In order to test the accuracy of the ﬁnal model, the input data is split into train- ing and testing data for the sake of fair testing and model validation. The test data set constitutes an entire average solar cycle length, none of which has been seen by the model in the training data set. Keeping an entire set of varied solar cycle conditions unseen and using this for validation ensures we evaluate the model’s ability to extrapolate to new behaviour. The training data set covers 14.5 years, most of solar cycle 23, and runs from May 1992 till October 2006, while the test set covers the 11 years from October 2006 till October 2017, which is the end of solar cycle 23 and a large part of 24. The machine learning method chosen for this study relies on Gradient Boosting Re- gressors (GBRs), and the speciﬁc implementation applied here is the Python version of XGBoost (Chen & Guestrin, 2016). The paper is published in The Astrophysical Journal (ApJ), 927, pp. 187 (2022), with DOI 10.3847/1538-4357/ac4af6. The lead author is Evangelia Samara, with co-authors including Brecht Laperre, Rungployphan Kieokaew, Manuela Temmer, Christine Verbeke, Luciano Rodriguez, Jasmina Magdalenić, and Stefaan Poedts.

The paper proposes dynamic time warping as an alternative way to score space weather models against observations, mainly for solar wind time series. It is also available as an arXiv preprint (2109.07873), first submitted in September 2021 and revised in February 2022. The authors test the method on WIND observations and EUHFORIA model output at Earth. The first application yields a similarity score, and the second measures timing and amplitude offsets between best-matched points. The authors describe it as a hybrid between correlation-style metrics and point-by-point comparison.

I couldn't find the specific 2023 Solar Physics paper by Milošić, Temmer, and Heinemann. The results include related work, so I'd treat these as context rather than the paper itself.

- **Milošić et al. (EGU 2022 abstract):** Milošić, Temmer, Heinemann and colleagues describe an upgraded Empirical Solar Wind Forecast model. It is an ESA service that forecasts solar wind speed at Earth with a 4-day lead time, and the authors add compression and rarefaction effects to better shape high-speed stream profiles. They present a statistical analysis for the period 2012 - 2019 showing that their adaptations improve the ability to predict HSS speed profiles as well as smaller structures. This abstract is the closest match I found, but it is not the 2023 paper.

- **EUHFORIA comparison (a 2024 arXiv paper, not by this group):** That paper compares a machine-learning coronal-hole model against EUHFORIA for November 2017 to September 2019. It reports that it outperforms EUHFORIA in all metrics by a large margin. It also notes that EUHFORIA uses static empirical relationships to set the properties of the young solar wind, i.e., it does not adapt well to the current state of the Sun.

- **Heinemann's earlier work:** Heinemann's 2018 arXiv paper on coronal holes describes high-speed streams as the fast plasma outflow from those localized coronal areas, linked to increased solar wind speed in interplanetary space.

- **EUHFORIA background (Hinterreiter et al., 2019, Solar Physics):** This evaluation found that for the low-activity phase a better match between model results and observations held compared with the high-activity interval.

To find the 2023 paper itself, search the Solar Physics journal (Springer) or ADS using the title keywords and "empirical solar wind forecast."
